systems.name: Integumentary
systems.description: The skin and its appendages form the body's outer barrier. It protects against injury, infection and water loss, regulates temperature and houses touch receptors.

systems.name: Skeletal
systems.description: Bones, cartilage and joints that support the body, protect organs, anchor muscles and store minerals. Marrow inside certain bones produces blood cells.

systems.name: Muscular
systems.description: Skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle that generate movement, maintain posture and produce heat. Skeletal muscles work in pairs, pulling on bones through tendons.

systems.name: Nervous
systems.description: The brain, spinal cord and peripheral nerves carry electrical signals that coordinate sensation, thought, movement and automatic functions.

systems.name: Endocrine
systems.description: Glands that release hormones into the blood to regulate metabolism, growth, stress response, mood and reproduction.

systems.name: Cardiovascular
systems.description: The heart and blood vessels circulate blood, delivering oxygen and nutrients to tissues and carrying away carbon dioxide and wastes.

systems.name: Lymphatic
systems.description: A network of vessels, nodes and organs that drains excess tissue fluid back to the blood and filters it for pathogens and debris.

systems.name: Immune
systems.description: Cells, tissues and organs that recognise and eliminate pathogens, abnormal cells and foreign material, and remember past threats.

systems.name: Respiratory
systems.description: The airways, lungs and breathing muscles that bring oxygen in, remove carbon dioxide, and help regulate blood pH.

systems.name: Digestive
systems.description: The gastrointestinal tract and accessory organs that break food down, absorb nutrients and water, and eliminate solid waste.

systems.name: Urinary
systems.description: Kidneys, ureters and bladder filter blood, balance fluids, electrolytes and acidity, and remove waste as urine.

systems.name: Reproductive
systems.description: Organs and glands responsible for producing gametes and sex hormones, and, in females, supporting pregnancy.

structures.description: The skin of the scalp and face is rich in blood vessels, hair follicles and sebaceous glands. It protects underlying tissue and is highly sensitive to touch and temperature.
facts: Facial skin is among the thinnest on the body.
Skin is the body's largest organ.

structures.description: Thin, flexible skin that stretches with head movement. It covers the airway and major vessels passing between head and trunk.
facts: Skin is the body's largest organ.
The epidermis renews itself roughly every 4 weeks.

structures.description: The skin over the chest, abdomen and back. It forms a waterproof barrier and helps regulate body temperature through sweating and blood flow.
facts: Back skin is up to four times thicker than the eyelids.
Skin is the body's largest organ.
The epidermis renews itself roughly every 4 weeks.

structures.description: The skin of the upper limb protects underlying muscle and nerves and contains sweat glands that cool the body during activity.
facts: Skin is the body's largest organ.
The epidermis renews itself roughly every 4 weeks.

structures.description: The skin of the upper limb protects underlying muscle and nerves and contains sweat glands that cool the body during activity.
facts: Skin is the body's largest organ.
The epidermis renews itself roughly every 4 weeks.

structures.description: The skin of the lower limb is thick enough to withstand friction and pressure, and contains sweat glands and sensory receptors.
facts: Skin is the body's largest organ.
The epidermis renews itself roughly every 4 weeks.

structures.description: A bony structure of 22 bones that encloses and protects the brain and supports the face. Most of its bones are fused by tight, immovable joints called sutures.
facts: Only the mandible (jaw) is freely movable.
Adult skull bones are joined by sutures that were open in infancy.

structures.description: A stack of 33 vertebrae separated by cartilage discs that supports the trunk and encases the spinal cord. Its S-shaped curves absorb shock and keep the body balanced.
facts: Has cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral and coccygeal regions.
Intervertebral discs make up about a quarter of spinal length.

structures.description: Twelve pairs of ribs joined to the thoracic vertebrae and, mostly, the sternum. It shields the heart and lungs and flexes during breathing.
facts: The first seven pairs attach directly to the sternum.
The lowest two pairs are "floating" and do not attach at the front.

structures.description: A ring of bones that transfers the weight of the upper body to the legs and cradles the lower abdominal organs. It is typically broader and shallower in females to allow childbirth.
facts: Formed by the two hip bones, sacrum and coccyx.
Pelvic shape is one of the most reliable skeletal indicators of sex.

structures.description: The long bone of the upper arm, connecting the shoulder to the elbow. It is the attachment point for the deltoid, biceps and triceps.
facts: The radial nerve runs in a groove along its shaft.
Fractures can injure this nerve.

structures.description: The long bone of the upper arm, connecting the shoulder to the elbow. It is the attachment point for the deltoid, biceps and triceps.
facts: The radial nerve runs in a groove along its shaft.
Fractures can injure this nerve.

structures.description: The thigh bone, and the longest, strongest bone in the body. It bears the body's weight during standing, walking and running.
facts: Accounts for roughly a quarter of body height.
Can withstand forces of many times body weight.

structures.description: The thigh bone, and the longest, strongest bone in the body. It bears the body's weight during standing, walking and running.
facts: Accounts for roughly a quarter of body height.
Can withstand forces of many times body weight.

structures.description: The shin bone, the larger of the two lower-leg bones. It carries most of the weight transmitted from the knee to the ankle.
facts: Its front edge sits just under the skin.
The fibula beside it bears little weight.

The fibula beside it bears little weight.

structures.description: Soft tissue inside bone cavities, such as the iliac crest of the pelvis. Red marrow produces red cells, platelets and white cells, making it both a skeletal tissue and a core organ of the immune system.
facts: Produces roughly 500 billion blood cells every day.
Red marrow is replaced by fatty yellow marrow in many adult bones.

structures.description: A broad, fan-shaped chest muscle that adducts and rotates the arm inward. It is a major muscle of pushing movements.
facts: Attaches to the clavicle, sternum and upper ribs.
Assists forced inspiration when the arm is fixed.

structures.description: A broad, fan-shaped chest muscle that adducts and rotates the arm inward. It is a major muscle of pushing movements.
facts: Attaches to the clavicle, sternum and upper ribs.
Assists forced inspiration when the arm is fixed.

structures.description: A two-headed muscle on the front of the upper arm. It flexes the elbow and rotates the forearm so the palm faces up.
facts: "Biceps" means two heads.
Its tendon can rupture at the shoulder or elbow.

structures.description: A two-headed muscle on the front of the upper arm. It flexes the elbow and rotates the forearm so the palm faces up.
facts: "Biceps" means two heads.
Its tendon can rupture at the shoulder or elbow.

structures.description: A group of four muscles on the front of the thigh that extend the knee. They are among the largest and most powerful muscles in the body.
facts: Includes rectus femoris and three vastus muscles.
Essential for standing up, climbing and jumping.

structures.description: A group of four muscles on the front of the thigh that extend the knee. They are among the largest and most powerful muscles in the body.
facts: Includes rectus femoris and three vastus muscles.
Essential for standing up, climbing and jumping.

structures.description: A dome-shaped sheet of skeletal muscle beneath the lungs. When it contracts and flattens, the chest expands and air is drawn into the lungs, making it the main muscle of breathing.
facts: Does about 70% of the work of quiet breathing.
Hiccups are involuntary spasms of the diaphragm.

structures.description: The control centre of the body, made of about 86 billion neurons. It processes sensory input, forms thoughts and memories, and directs movement and automatic functions.
facts: Uses roughly 20% of the body's energy at rest.
Weighs about 1.3 kg in adults.

structures.description: A long bundle of nerve tissue running within the vertebral column. It relays signals between the brain and body and coordinates simple reflexes without involving the brain.
facts: About 45 cm long in adults.
31 pairs of spinal nerves branch from it.

structures.description: The longest and thickest nerve in the body, running from the lower spine through the buttock and down the back of the leg. It controls hamstring muscles and carries sensation from the leg and foot.
facts: Nearly as wide as a thumb at its origin.
Compression can cause the pain known as sciatica.

structures.description: The longest and thickest nerve in the body, running from the lower spine through the buttock and down the back of the leg. It controls hamstring muscles and carries sensation from the leg and foot.
facts: Nearly as wide as a thumb at its origin.
Compression can cause the pain known as sciatica.

structures.description: A pea-sized gland at the base of the brain, often called the "master gland". It releases hormones that control growth, other endocrine glands, water balance and lactation.
facts: Controlled by the hypothalamus above it.
About the size of a pea.

structures.description: A butterfly-shaped gland in the front of the neck. Its hormones set the body's metabolic rate, influencing heart rate, temperature and energy use.
facts: Needs iodine to make thyroid hormone.
Sits just below the larynx, wrapped around the trachea.

structures.description: A small gland perched on top of each kidney. It releases cortisol, adrenaline and aldosterone, hormones that govern stress response, blood pressure and salt balance.
facts: The outer cortex and inner medulla make different hormones.
Adrenaline raises heart rate within seconds.

structures.description: A small gland perched on top of each kidney. It releases cortisol, adrenaline and aldosterone, hormones that govern stress response, blood pressure and salt balance.
facts: The outer cortex and inner medulla make different hormones.
Adrenaline raises heart rate within seconds.

structures.description: A long gland behind the stomach with two jobs. Its exocrine cells release digestive enzymes into the small intestine, while islet cells release insulin and glucagon to control blood sugar.
facts: Insulin is made by beta cells in the islets of Langerhans.
Releases about 1 litre of digestive juice per day.

structures.description: A four-chambered muscular pump about the size of a fist. It beats roughly 100,000 times a day, sending oxygen-poor blood to the lungs and oxygen-rich blood to the rest of the body.
facts: Pumps about 5 litres of blood per minute at rest.
Has four valves that keep blood flowing one way.

structures.description: The largest artery in the body, rising from the left ventricle and arching down through the chest and abdomen. It distributes oxygenated blood to nearly every organ.
facts: About 2.5 cm wide in adults.
Branches supply the head, arms, organs and legs.

structures.description: The large vein that returns blood from the lower body to the right atrium of the heart. It runs up alongside the spine, to the right of the aorta.
facts: Carries blood from the legs, pelvis and abdomen.
Its flow is aided by leg muscles and breathing.

structures.description: A small gland behind the breastbone where T lymphocytes mature. It is most active in childhood and gradually shrinks and is replaced by fat with age.
facts: "T cells" are named for the thymus.
Largest relative to body size in infancy.

structures.description: A fist-sized organ in the upper left abdomen. It filters old red blood cells from the blood, stores platelets, and houses white cells that respond to blood-borne infections.
facts: Lies under the ribs, so it is protected but can be injured.
People can live without a spleen, with higher infection risk.

structures.description: Bean-shaped filters in the armpit that drain the arm, chest wall and breast. Immune cells inside trap and respond to pathogens carried in lymph.
facts: Swell when fighting infection nearby.
Commonly examined in breast cancer staging.

structures.description: Bean-shaped filters in the armpit that drain the arm, chest wall and breast. Immune cells inside trap and respond to pathogens carried in lymph.
facts: Swell when fighting infection nearby.

structures.description: Lymph nodes in the groin that filter fluid draining from the legs, genitals and lower abdominal wall.
facts: Often swell with infections in the foot or leg.
The body holds 600-700 lymph nodes in total.

structures.description: Lymph nodes in the groin that filter fluid draining from the legs, genitals and lower abdominal wall.

The body holds 600-700 lymph nodes in total.

structures.description: The windpipe, a tube about 10-12 cm long reinforced by C-shaped cartilage rings. It carries air from the larynx down to the bronchi, and its lining traps and clears inhaled particles.
facts: Splits into the left and right bronchi.
Cilia sweep mucus upward toward the throat.

structures.description: The left lung has two lobes and a notch, the cardiac notch, that makes room for the heart. Millions of tiny air sacs in its tissue transfer oxygen into the blood.
facts: Slightly smaller than the right lung.
Contains around 150 million alveoli.

structures.description: The right lung has three lobes and is a little larger than the left. It exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide across the thin walls of its alveoli.
facts: Alveoli provide a surface area of roughly 70 m².
Air entering the right bronchus has a steeper path.

structures.description: A muscular tube about 25 cm long that carries swallowed food from the throat to the stomach. Waves of contraction called peristalsis push food along, even upside down.
facts: Passes through the diaphragm to reach the stomach.
Has a sphincter at each end.

structures.description: A J-shaped muscular bag that churns food with acid and enzymes into a semi-liquid called chyme. Its acidic environment also kills most swallowed microbes.
facts: Can hold about 1-1.5 litres.
Its lining replaces itself every few days.

structures.description: The body's largest internal organ, sitting in the upper right abdomen. It makes bile for fat digestion, processes nutrients absorbed from the gut, detoxifies the blood and stores glycogen.
facts: Performs over 500 known functions.
Can regenerate after partial removal.
Weighs about 1.5 kg in adults.

structures.description: A small pouch under the liver that stores and concentrates bile. It squeezes bile into the small intestine after a fatty meal.
facts: Holds about 50 mL of bile.
Not essential: people live normally without it.

structures.description: A coiled tube roughly 6 metres long where most digestion and nutrient absorption occurs. Its folded lining is covered in villi that vastly increase its surface area.
facts: Has three parts: duodenum, jejunum and ileum.
Absorbs most nutrients from food.

structures.description: A wide tube about 1.5 metres long framing the small intestine. It absorbs water and electrolytes from remaining waste, forms stool, and hosts trillions of gut bacteria.
facts: Includes the colon, cecum and rectum.
Gut bacteria help make some vitamins.

structures.description: A bean-shaped organ about the size of a fist, tucked against the back wall of the abdomen. Each contains about a million nephrons that filter blood, balance fluids and make urine.
facts: Filters around 180 litres of blood plasma a day.
Also makes hormones that control blood pressure and red-cell production.

structures.description: A bean-shaped organ about the size of a fist, tucked against the back wall of the abdomen. Each contains about a million nephrons that filter blood, balance fluids and make urine.
facts: Filters around 180 litres of blood plasma a day.
Also makes hormones that control blood pressure and red-cell production.

structures.description: A narrow muscular tube about 25 cm long that carries urine from the kidney to the bladder using rhythmic waves of contraction.
facts: Enters the bladder at a slant to prevent backflow.
Roughly 3-4 mm wide.

structures.description: A narrow muscular tube about 25 cm long that carries urine from the kidney to the bladder using rhythmic waves of contraction.

structures.description: A stretchy muscular sac in the pelvis that stores urine. It signals the urge to urinate as it fills and contracts to expel urine through the urethra.
facts: Typically holds 400-600 mL.
Its wall is lined with specialised, stretchable cells.

structures.description: One of two oval glands in the scrotum that produce sperm and testosterone. The scrotum keeps them slightly cooler than core body temperature, which sperm production requires.
facts: Sperm take about 70 days to develop.
Testosterone is also made here.

Testosterone is also made here.

structures.description: A walnut-sized gland below the bladder that surrounds the urethra. It adds fluid to semen that nourishes and protects sperm.
facts: Tends to enlarge with age.
Makes about a third of semen volume.

structures.description: A hollow, pear-shaped muscular organ in the pelvis. Its lining thickens each cycle to receive a fertilised egg, and it expands to hold a growing fetus during pregnancy.
facts: The inner lining is shed during menstruation.
Can expand to hold a full-term baby, then return to near-original size.

structures.description: An almond-sized organ on each side of the uterus that stores and releases eggs and produces estrogen and progesterone.
facts: Females are born with roughly 1-2 million immature eggs.
Typically releases one egg per cycle, alternating sides.
